item.title: What do two firsts in China's NEV industry mean?
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
What do two firsts in China's NEV industry mean? Technicians carry out quality inspections in the general assembly workshop of an auto factory of Chinese automobile manufacturer Lynk & Co. in Yiwu, east China's Zhejiang province. (Photo/Chen Ye) In July, new energy vehicles (NEVs) accounted for more than 60 percent of monthly new vehicle sales in China for the first time, while their share of cumulative sales surpassed 50 percent for the first time. These two milestones, highlighted in the latest data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), have drawn particular attention. To grasp the significance of these achievements, it is useful to consider two recent rankings that made headlines. In July, NEV models occupied nine of the top 10 best-selling passenger vehicle models in China's retail market. In the first half of the year, three Chinese automakers, leveraging their strengths in NEV technologies, entered the global top 10 automotive brands for the first time, collectively joining the industry's first tier. These figures show that, after years of development, NEVs have crossed the critical threshold of accounting for more than half of the market and have become a mainstream choice for consumers. As an essential path for China to move from a major automobile producer to a global automotive powerhouse, this landmark shift in market structure represents another step toward that goal. Gear boxes for new energy vehicles are manufactured on a smart production line at a factory of ACTECO Powertrain in Wuhu, east China's Anhui province. (Photo/Xiao Benxiang) How did these two milestones come about? First, products have become increasingly competitive. Advances in power batteries, smart cabins and driver-assistance systems, combined with continued improvements in cost-effectiveness, intelligent features and safety, have further strengthened the appeal of NEVs. In the first year of the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), many domestic brands have leveraged their strong technological capabilities to expand into new market segments while moving up the value chain, breaking into the high-end market and gaining a firm foothold. Second, market demand remains strong. NEVs accounted for more than half of China's vehicle exports for two consecutive months, with export growth outpacing that of conventional fuel-powered vehicles. Since the beginning of this year, NEV exports have become a key driver of the overall auto industry and an important engine driving export growth. Many analysts believe the momentum will continue, with full-year NEV exports expected to exceed four million units. Third, relevant infrastructure has continued to improve. As of the end of June, China had 23.057 million electric vehicle charging points, up 43.2 percent year on year, with charging facilities covering 98.61 percent of counties nationwide. A consumer tries out a new energy vehicle at a car dealership in Zhangjiagang, east China's Jiangsu province. (Photo/Xing Bin) The world's largest vehicle charging network and the most complete NEV industrial chain have become increasingly interconnected and mutually reinforcing, providing strong support and resilience for the continued growth of the NEV industry. The two milestones also mark a new starting point. The development of NEVs has become a common priority in industrial planning across many regions. A review of the 15th Five-Year Plan outlines of all 31 provincial-level regions shows that intelligent connected NEVs have been identified as an important area for cultivating new quality productive forces. Over the next five years, localities are expected to build on their respective strengths and pursue differentiated development, creating further room for China's NEV industry to grow. As the domestic market landscape becomes increasingly clear, the global automotive industry is also undergoing an accelerated transformation. By staying committed to innovation, improving product quality and strengthening brands, China has established a modern automotive industry system that is self-reliant, controllable, safe, efficient, green, intelligent, and globally competitive. The momentum is already building, and further growth is within reach. Chinese cars are expected to achieve futher breakthroughs. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Japan's right-wing revisionists will ultimately face historical reckoning
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Japan's right-wing revisionists will ultimately face historical reckoning August 15 marks the day Japan surrendered in World War II. It is a day that commemorates the victory of the World Anti-Fascist War and serves as a solemn reminder to remember history and safeguard peace. Yet on this very day, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a ritual offering to the Yasukuni Shrine, a site that honors Class-A war criminals from World War II. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, along with three other serving Cabinet members, the secretary-general and other senior officials of the Liberal Democratic Party, and approximately 90 lawmakers from the cross-party parliamentary group "The Assembly of Diet Members to Visit Yasukuni Shrine Together," also paid their respects there. This series of regressive actions once again exposes the Takaichi administration's sinister intent to distort the history of aggression and glorify militarism. It constitutes a blatant affront to historical justice, a grave insult to the feelings of people in Asian countries that suffered under Japanese aggression, and a deliberate provocation against the outcome of World War II and the postwar international order. Unsurprisingly, it has drawn strong condemnation from the international community and conscientious voices within Japan itself. Japanese politicians' visits to Yasukuni Shrine are by no means merely a matter of personal religious belief or Japan's internal affairs. They touch upon a fundamental question: whether Japan will honor its postwar commitment to peace and correctly confront its history of aggression. Yasukuni Shrine is never an ordinary religious site. It served as a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism during its wars of external aggression. The 14 Class-A war criminals enshrined there were wartime culprits whose hands were stained with the blood of people across Asia. History has repeatedly shown that sincerely reflecting on the history of aggression and thoroughly eliminating the legacy of militarism are important political foundations for Japan to develop constructive relations with its Asian neighbors. An editorial in Japan's Asahi Shimbun noted that such actions undermine Japan's postwar pacifist principles and constitutional order, and damage political trust between Japan and neighboring countries such as China and South Korea. The disgraceful actions of right-wing politicians such as Takaichi and Koizumi are not merely a short-term political stunt. They are a concentrated manifestation of their deeply rooted historical revisionism. In her speech at the national memorial service for the war dead held on August 15, Takaichi deliberately downplayed the devastating suffering inflicted by Japanese militarism on other Asian countries, making no mention of "remorse" or "lessons learned." Instead, she selectively highlighted Japan's so-called "wartime sacrifices," deliberately portraying Japan as a victim of the war. This distortion of history is consistent with her conduct earlier at ceremonies commemorating the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. She also remained ambiguous about whether Japan should continue to uphold its Three Non-Nuclear Principles. This distorted logic of emphasizing only a "victim narrative" while severing Japan's identity as an aggressor is a familiar tactic used by Japan's right-wing forces to evade responsibility for and whitewash the history of aggression. Takaichi is now pushing this reactionary current from the shadows into the open and from the margins toward the mainstream. Japanese Communist Party secretary general Akira Koike hit the nail on the head, saying that Takaichi spoke as if she were the leader of a country that had suffered aggression. A country that refuses to reflect on its past cannot earn the trust of the international community. Distorted perceptions of history inevitably lead to misguided policies in the present. Invoking the spirit of militarism ultimately serves the purpose of paving the way for further easing of restriction on Japan's military. In recent years, Japan has continuously broken through the constraints of its postwar pacifist framework, substantially increased its defense budget for consecutive years, accelerated the development of what it calls "counterstrike capabilities," promoted exports of lethal weapons and steadily hollowed out the principle of "exclusively defense-oriented policy." It has gone further and further down the road of military expansion. The decision by Takaichi and other Japanese right-wing politicians to glorify militarism on the anniversary of Japan's surrender is ultimately aimed at manufacturing public support and rallying public opinion behind efforts to break through the constraints of the postwar system and push ahead with military expansion and war preparations. Nevertheless, right-wing politicians who seek to turn back the clock of history cannot represent the Japanese people. On August 15, large numbers of Japanese people spontaneously held rallies and marches, urging the government to face up to its history of aggression and deeply reflect on its wartime crimes. They also criticized the right-wing politicians for ignoring people's livelihoods and pursuing a misguided policy of militarization. Atsushi Koketsu, professor emeritus at Yamaguchi University, pointed out that the Japanese government's drive for "remilitarization" comes at the expense of the interests of its people. Trading people's anxiety about their livelihoods for so-called "national security" is fundamentally the wrong path for development. An editorial in Tokyo Shimbun warned that many of the policies promoted by Takaichi show clear signs of a "return to the prewar era." Measures to revitalize the military industry and expand Japan's armed forces bear strong similarities to prewar Japan. Without timely correction, the achievements of postwar democracy could be squandered. This year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial. The trial was an important outcome of the victory in the World Anti-Fascist War and laid a legal foundation for the postwar international order. Its justice and authority brook no challenge or revisionist reinterpretation. The actions of the Takaichi administration amount, in essence, to an open denial of the outcome of World War II and the postwar international order. Turning back the clock of history can only lead to repeating past mistakes; betraying historical justice will ultimately invite judgment by history. Japan's only right path is to squarely face up to its history of aggression, draw profound lessons from the war, completely break with militarism and remain committed to the path of peaceful development. That is the only sound foundation for Japan's future. (Zhong Sheng is a pen name often used by People's Daily to express its views on foreign policy and international affairs.) item.title: China's robots: Don't just watch, understand the industrial system
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
China's robots: Don't just watch, understand the industrial system Illustration: Chen Xia/GT A Chinese humanoid robot clocked 9.39 seconds to beat the men's 100m world record of 9.58 seconds set by Usain Bolt. This feat, achieved during the opening ceremony of the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, quickly captured global headlines. The second World Humanoid Robot Games offered a vivid window into the country's fast-moving robotics industry. Images of humanoid machines running, balancing, navigating obstacles and performing coordinated tasks naturally attract attention. Such events reveal something significant: China has become exceptionally capable of translating advances in components, controls, software integration and manufacturing into physical machines that can be built, tested and improved at speed. The value of these competitions lies less in a single headline-grabbing performance than in the industrial system behind it. A humanoid robot on a track is the visible result of motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, structural materials, motion-control systems, embedded software, training data, assembly processes and field maintenance working together. China's advantage increasingly lies in its ability to coordinate the entire supply chain. It has a broad base of electronics and machinery suppliers, strong manufacturing capacity, dense industrial clusters, and a large pool of potential users willing to test robots in factories, warehouses, ports, shops, hospitals and service settings. Competitions can therefore serve as public demonstrations and stress tests for a wider ecosystem. This development has occurred amid expanding US restrictions on China's access to advanced technologies, particularly leading-edge semiconductors, high-performance computing equipment and certain software and manufacturing tools. These measures have had real effects. They raise costs, complicate supply chains and make it harder for Chinese firms to obtain some of the most advanced chips and technical capabilities. Robotics increasingly depends on artificial intelligence, high-performance processors and sophisticated development tools, and US containment policy has challenged China's robotics development. Yet the restrictions have not stopped China's robotics industry from growing. One reason is that industrial competitiveness is not determined by frontier chips alone. In many robotics applications, the decisive challenge is making a system reliable, affordable, maintainable and safe in real operating conditions. China's large and varied domestic market provides companies with unusually frequent opportunities to confront these challenges. A robot deployed in a logistics center, manufacturing workshop or pharmacy generates feedback that can improve design, software, hardware integration and service procedures. This creates a reinforcing cycle: More applications produce more operational data and experience; better products reduce costs and increase confidence; and lower costs support wider deployment. Scale matters as well. China's manufacturing ecosystem enables firms to move from prototype to small-batch production and then to larger-scale delivery relatively quickly. That process can accelerate learning not only for robot makers but also for suppliers of actuators, sensors, machine vision systems, batteries and precision components. The result is not simply a lower-cost version of foreign technology. It is a growing capacity to adapt products to diverse use cases and to iterate rapidly when products encounter real-world constraints. This has implications beyond China. As robots become more available and affordable, they can help manufacturers globally address labor shortages, improve workplace safety and raise productivity in repetitive or hazardous tasks. Chinese firms can contribute equipment, components and competitive pressure that expand the overall market and reduce barriers to adoption. In this sense, China's robotics progress may become part of a broader modernization of global manufacturing rather than a purely national achievement. However, a balanced assessment requires acknowledging the remaining gaps. The US retains major strengths in foundational artificial intelligence research, advanced semiconductors, computing platforms and software ecosystems. Japan and several European countries remain highly competitive in precision components, industrial reliability, specialized automation, safety systems and technical standards. China still faces challenges in certain high-end chips, core software, advanced sensors, precision parts, long-term reliability, and internationally recognized standards and certification. China's recent robotics events deserve attention because they illustrate a broader industrial fact. Despite external technological constraints, China has leveraged its domestic market, supply-chain depth, engineering talent and manufacturing scale to strengthen its position in robotics. Its advantage lies not in claiming technological supremacy in every category, but in its growing ability to turn innovation into deployment. If China can continue to close its remaining gaps while remaining open to global collaboration and standards, its robotics industry could become an important contributor to the next phase of worldwide industrial development. item.title: Retired U.S. teacher begins China visit to renew friendship kindled in classroom, taming of desert
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Retired U.S. teacher begins China visit to renew friendship kindled in classroom, taming of desert Yin Yuzhen is reunited with Ronald Sakolsky at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who once supported China's desertification control efforts, arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a visit aimed at renewing a friendship with the Chinese people that first took root more than two decades ago. The 69-year-old will spend part of his stay planting trees alongside his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land for four decades. Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries. After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification. At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life. The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees. In May this year, Yin took to the internet in search of the American friend who had offered the donation decades ago, and their online reunion, a moment that moved many, soon followed. On May 18, the two finally connected over a video call. Yin, who had been practicing over and over, greeted him in her slightly broken English: "You are brother!" Upon arriving in Beijing, Sakolsky said he was eager to meet Yin in northern China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, reconnect with former colleagues and students, and see the forest with his own eyes. He also received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the desert. Ahead of Sakolsky's arrival in Inner Mongolia on Sunday afternoon, Yin, no less excited, brought with her pepino melons freshly picked from her orchard. "I went to pick some pepino melons for him, so he can taste the fruit from the desert the moment he steps off the plane," she said. "When I tell him I grew these in the desert, he won't believe it." Yin Yuzhen waves to Ronald Sakolsky at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) At the Ordos Ejin Horo Airport in Inner Mongolia, as soon as Yin spotted him coming down the escalator, she rushed to him. Overcome with emotion, the two hugged tightly, weeping with joy after more than two decades apart. "This is a dream come true," said Sakolsky. "She made a promise 27 years ago and she kept her promise. I never thought I would see her again. It is a miracle, but it shows culture and people can still keep promises." Invited by the China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE), his itinerary from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1 will also include China-U.S. teacher exchange events, a visit to Henan to meet with teachers and students at the school where he worked, a visit to the press briefing hall of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and visits to historical and cultural landmarks. The invitation is intended to further promote China-U.S. educational exchanges, convey the Chinese people's deep appreciation of friendship, and inspire more people to carry forward heartwarming stories of goodwill between the two peoples, a CEAIE official said. Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns. Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students. Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu (about 10.13 million hectares) of sandified land between 2021 and 2025. item.title: China's global initiatives offer new opportunities for cooperation, says Italian business leader
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
China's global initiatives offer new opportunities for cooperation, says Italian business leader Guests attend the 4th China-Italy Friendship Cities Cooperation Dialogue in Rome, Italy, April 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Jing) ROME, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The China-proposed four global initiatives offer a new perspective on international governance and new opportunities for international cooperation amid geopolitical fragmentation and global instability, said an Italian business leader. The initiatives represent China's efforts to provide coordinated responses to challenges that transcend national borders, Mario Boselli, president of the Italy-China Foundation, said in a recent interview with Xinhua. They also represent a deepening of China's international vision following more than a decade of the Belt and Road Initiative, extending the focus from economic and infrastructure cooperation to development, security, dialogue among civilizations and global governance, he said. He believes that the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI) could offer opportunities to deepen cooperation between China and Europe, including Italy. The GDI's focus on climate change, the UN Sustainable Development Goals, digitalization and technological innovation could create opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy, photovoltaics and energy storage, among others, said Boselli. Italy and China can also strengthen cooperation among universities and research institutions in biotechnology, healthcare, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, he added. Noting that the GCI could promote cooperation in culture, heritage conservation, universities and youth exchanges, he said Italy, with its rich cultural heritage and the strong appeal of "Made in Italy" in China, is "one of the most natural European partners" for such initiatives. Taken together, the four initiatives outline a vision of a multipolar world with greater participation by emerging economies and countries of the Global South, Boselli said. With its tradition of dialogue with China and complementary economic strengths, Italy can play a bridging role between China and Europe, promoting practical cooperation in sustainable development, innovation, culture and global governance, he said. China's initiatives may not provide an immediate solution to current international tensions, but can offer "a space for reflection and dialogue" to identify more inclusive, practical and long-term forms of cooperation, he added. item.title: Three hydrological stations reveal China's efforts to protect the Yellow River
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Three hydrological stations reveal China's efforts to protect the Yellow River The Yellow River is China's second-largest river. Yet the "mother river" once faced severe water shortages. Between 1972 and 1996, it ran dry for 19 years. Since 1999, China has implemented unified water allocation and regulation along the Yellow River, enacted the Yellow River Protection Law, and most recently incorporated relevant provisions into the newly adopted Ecological and Environmental Code. These measures have steadily strengthened the river's protection framework. As a result, the Yellow River has maintained continuous flow for 27 consecutive years, and ecological conservation and high-quality development across its basin have entered a new phase. More than 180 hydrological stations along the Yellow River serve as the river's "eyes," bearing witness to the transformation of the mighty waterway. Examining three of these stations illustrates how China is working to protect its major rivers. A hydrologist from the Madoi Hydrological Team conducts comparative gauging tests for new instruments and equipment. (Photo/Liu Wenzhou) Huangheyan Hydrological Station, Madoi, Qinghai Province Zhaling Lake and Eling Lake are known as the "sister lakes" at the source of the Yellow River. Along their shores, hydrological monitoring equipment equipped with the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System tracks changes in water levels. "We can receive hydrological data around the clock," said Li Peiyan, deputy head of the Madoi hydrological team of the Yellow River Conservancy Commission. The Madoi team oversees six stations, including those at Zhaling Lake, Eling Lake, and Huangheyan. Situated at an elevation of about 4,300 meters, Huangheyan Hydrological Station is the closest to the Yellow River's source and the highest hydrological station in the basin. "In the past, our team members had to carry equipment into the water to measure flow. In the bitter cold, they would stand in the water for two or three hours at a time," Li said. "Now, with equipment such as radar-based online flow measurement systems in operation, our team members no longer need to enter the water, and monitoring and reporting have become much more efficient." From 2000 to 2025, the Huangheyan station recorded fluctuations in runoff, with a period of relatively low flows followed by higher flows. Runoff has increased significantly in recent years. China has strengthened the protection of Zhaling Lake, Eling Lake, and other rivers and lakes while intensifying desertification control in key areas. As a result, the water conservation capacity of the Yellow River source region has continued to improve. The Sanjiangyuan region now conserves 40.895 billion cubic meters of water annually. Keeping the Yellow River flowing for 27 consecutive years has also required comprehensive management of water conservation, use, and protection. China has moved from unregulated water diversion to unified water allocation and regulation, and from excessive water use to intensive water conservation and control. Fourteen mandatory national standards for water-use quotas in the Yellow River basin have come into force, curbing unreasonable water demand and establishing a water-use quota system covering major crops, industrial products, and consumer services sector. At Longmen Hydrological Station, a sounding-weight carries a shipboard‑type Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler to measure discharge. (Photo/Lu Yang) Longmen Hydrological Station, Hancheng, Shaanxi Province The Longmen Hydrological Station of the Yellow River Conservancy Commission is perched on a cliff at the downstream end of the Shanxi-Shaanxi Gorge. During the flood season, Liu Jinyang, head of the station's data processing team, and his colleagues remain on duty around the clock, closely monitoring fluctuations in the river level. "Discharge at the monitoring section is 1,300 cubic meters per second, while the online photoelectric sediment monitor records a sediment concentration of 50 kilograms per cubic meter," Liu said. The data is transmitted directly to the Yellow River flood control and dispatch center. "Accurate measurements depend largely on the new equipment," Liu said. In the water, a moving Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) measures discharge as it travels through the current. On shore, an image-based online flow measurement system uses cameras and algorithms to calculate discharge from visual data. In the sky, drones can fly back and forth between 12 monitoring points in just 15 minutes. "The different sets of data cross-check one another, making monitoring and reporting more accurate and helping us anticipate changes in river conditions," Liu said. Self-developed technologies, including online photoelectric sediment monitors and "smart guardians" for dams and riverbanks, have also been put into use. An integrated monitoring and sensing system combining satellites, drones, video surveillance and other technologies across the sky, air, ground, water and hydraulic infrastructure is being developed, while a digital twin system for the Yellow River continues to take shape. Years of development have brought the physical Yellow River, the model Yellow River and the digital-twin Yellow River into deeper integration and closer coordination. River management is shifting from relying on "experience-based assessment" to making "intelligent, data-driven predictions." Photo shows a section of the Yellow River in Pinglu county, Yuncheng, north China's Shanxi province. (Photo/Hao Jian) Lijin Hydrological Station, Dongying, Shandong Province Located in Dongying, east China's Shandong province, Lijin Hydrological Station is the last hydrological station before the Yellow River reaches the sea. From unified water allocation and regulation to water and sediment regulation and ecological water replenishment, the station shoulders a wide range of tasks. "We are the last pair of 'eyes' on the Yellow River before it reaches the sea. The results of Yellow River conservation and management can be seen in these data," said Xing Xijin, deputy head of the Lijin Hydrological Station. He pointed to a series of positive changes: the wetlands of the Yellow River Delta have steadily expanded, habitats for plants and animals have continued to improve, and biodiversity has increased significantly. The Yellow River Basin is rich in ecological resources and home to diverse species. Along the upper, middle and lower reaches, China has pursued systematic conservation of mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grasslands and deserts based on local conditions. In the upper reaches, China has strengthened the protection and restoration of key water sources to safeguard the "water tower of China." In the middle reaches, greater emphasis has been placed on soil and water conservation. In the lower reaches, efforts are accelerating to develop green ecological corridors and advance ecological conservation and restoration in the river estuary. Today, all 20 major control sections on the Yellow River's main stream and tributaries meet their ecological flow targets. In 2025, the soil and water conservation rate in the Yellow River Basin reached 69.75 percent, while the ecological condition of the basin's rivers and lakes has improved markedly.
